newsitem.title: USA: Fed says U.S. wage, price gains still moderate.
newsitem.headline: Fed says U.S. wage, price gains still moderate.

text.p: The Federal Reserve said on Wednesday that the U.S. economy continues to plough ahead with scant sign of any inflationary pressures.

In its latest Beige Book summary of national economic activity, the central banks described price pressures as "temperate" and said wage gains generally remained moderate despite tight labor markets throughout the country.
Fed policymakers will use the latest findings when they meet on March 25 to consider whether to raise interest rates for the first time in over two years.

U.S. bond prices rebounded from earlier losses immediately after the publication of the Beige Book as some investors bet that its results made a March 25 rate increase by the inflation-wary Fed less likely.
The Fed said that despite tight labor markets everywhere, wage gains showed no sign of breaking out of the 3-4 percent range that they have been in for the past several reports.

The Beige Book summary was prepared by the St Louis Fed bank and was based on interviews with businessmen before March 3. The last such survey of conditions in all 12 Fed regions was issued on Jan 22.

The Fed said that price increases at retailers and manufacturers were generally temperate, partly because stiff competition made it hard to boost prices. Some Fed districts said rising productivity was offsetting higher costs for wages and raw materials.
While wage gains were moderate, nearly every district reported difficulty finding and retaining new employees.

"Shortages of engineers and construction, skilled manufacturing and high-tech workers are most often noted," the Fed said. The Minneapolis Fed said there was "a feeding frenzy" for computer software experts.

Manufacturing activity was reported continuing at a generally high level and, in some cases, was growing. The Fed said there were only pockets of weakness, principally in industries like apparel where production was going overseas, and in paper and textile industries.
Retail sales were higher during February than a year ago in most districts with strong business for cosmetics, building materials, pharmaceuticals and home furnishings.
"Current inventories are generally at or slightly below desired levels," the Fed said, noting some reports of short supplies of popular new vehicles.

Demand for all types of loans, whether from consumers or real estate and commercial borrowers, was described as "decidedly mixed," though more Fed districts said loans were steady or falling than reported them on the rise.
Consumer loan requests, for example, were increasing at a slower rate in the Chicago Fed district but demand was mixed or flat in Atlanta and Cleveland.
"There appears to be no consistent trend in consumer loan quality," the Fed said, with delinquencies on the rise in the Cleveland and New York Fed districts but improving in Atlanta and Philadelphia.
Most districts said that prospects for livestock producers have brightened recently with fatter profit margins "the rule rather than the exception" for farmers.
